# Welcome

This lab introduces **Tabular Foundation Models** in R using **tabpfn** and shows how to expose predictive models as tools using **ellmer**.

## Learning objectives

- Train a TabPFN classifier
- Explore a realistic business dataset
- Wrap predictions in reusable R functions
- Register those functions as LLM tools
- Build a simple AI analyst

# Packages

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(gt)
library(rsample)
library(yardstick)
library(ellmer)
library(tabpfn)
library(contoso)
```

# Meet the Contoso data

```{r}
db <- create_contoso_duckdb(size = "small")

# view database! 
# contoso::launch_ui(db$con)

sales_df <- db$sales |> dplyr::collect()
View(sales_df)
```

## Define a prediction task

Rather than predicting raw profit, we'll create a binary outcome of high vs low margin orders.

```{r}
feature_data <- sales_df |>
  mutate(
    shipping_lag = as.numeric(delivery_date - order_date),
    is_online = if_else(store_key == 999999, 1, 0),
    
    # Standardize to USD
    gross_margin_usd = gross_margin / exchange_rate,
    discount_pct = if_else(gross_revenue > 0, discounts / gross_revenue, 0),
    
    # Target: Top quartile margin
    is_high_margin = factor(
      if_else(gross_margin_usd > quantile(gross_margin_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), "High", "Low"),
      levels = c("High", "Low")
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    is_high_margin,
    quantity,
    unit_price,
    discount_pct,
    shipping_lag,
    is_online,
    product_key,
    store_key
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na() |>
  dplyr::sample_frac(size = 0.01) # so folks can run this on their CPU quickly 
```

# What is TabPFN?

TabPFN stands for **Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network**.

It belongs to a newer family of models called **Tabular Foundation Models**. Instead of extensive hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN performs inference using a foundation model trained over millions of synthetic learning tasks. It supports classification and regression on many small-to-medium tabular datasets with minimal configuration.

# Train a model

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

model_data <- feature_data 

# our typical data split
data_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.8, strata = 'is_high_margin')
train_df <- training(data_split)
test_df  <- testing(data_split)

# x, y fit method
X_train <- select(train_df, -is_high_margin)
y_train <- train_df$is_high_margin

X_test <- select(test_df, -is_high_margin)
y_test <- test_df$is_high_margin
```

```{r}
# **this does not fit a model!**
# it stages the data for the forward pass on test, 
# it will also install the python dependencies the first time you call it & the pretrained checkpoint from huggingface. 
# additional setup notes such as user license requirements are listed on the tabpfn library README.
fit <- tab_pfn(X_train, y_train)
```

```{r}
pred <- predict(fit, X_test)

head(pred)
```

# Build a reusable one shot fit & predict function

```{r}
tabpfn_fit_and_predict_v1 <- \(train_df, test_df){

# same as above but within this special function
X_train <- select(train_df, -is_high_margin)
y_train <- train_df$is_high_margin

X_test <- select(test_df, -is_high_margin)
y_test <- test_df$is_high_margin

fit <- tab_pfn(X_train, y_train)

preds <- predict(fit, X_test)

    preds

}

tabpfn_fit_and_predict_v1(train_df, test_df)
```

# Introducing ellmer

ellmer provides a unified interface for LLM providers and supports tool calling from R.

```{r}
library(ellmer)

chat <- ellmer::chat("ollama/gemma4")

chat$chat("Hello! Please introduce yourself in one sentence.")
```

# Register the prediction tool

> **Note:** the chatbot provider & llm must be able to use 'tools' for this to work properly. 
even then, you might run into some issues. like below. 
```{r}
# Example

tabpfn_fit_and_predict_tool <- ellmer::tool(
  tabpfn_fit_and_predict_v1,
  name = "tabpfn_fit_and_predict_v1",
  description = "Predict whether a sale will be highly profitable.", 
  arguments = list(
               # ellmer::type_dataframe :'(
    train_df = ellmer::type_object("a dataframe such as 'training'"),
    test_df = ellmer::type_object("a dataframe such as 'test'")
  )
)

chat$register_tool(tabpfn_fit_and_predict_tool)

# this won't work
chat$chat("can you fit a tabpfn model for me? I have a train_df and test_df dataset, please help!")
```

# Register the tool, try again

tools prefer type number, type string, pass a data.frame 'name' not a dataframe_df object.
```{r}

tabpfn_fit_and_predict <- \(train_df_name, test_df_name, target_var) {
  # Resolve string names to active global environment objects
  train_df <- get(train_df_name, envir = .GlobalEnv)
  test_df  <- get(test_df_name, envir = .GlobalEnv)
  
  X_train <- select(train_df, -all_of(target_var))
  y_train <- train_df[[target_var]]
  
  X_test  <- select(test_df, -all_of(target_var))
  
  fit <- tab_pfn(X_train, y_train)
  predict(fit, X_test)
}

# Define the ellmer tool with string parameters
tabpfn_tool <- ellmer::tool(
  tabpfn_fit_and_predict,
  name = "tabpfn_fit_and_predict",
  description = "Fits a TabPFN model and predicts outcomes given in-memory R data frame object names.",
  arguments = list(
    train_df_name = ellmer::type_string("Name of the training data frame object in R memory (e.g. 'train_df')"),
    test_df_name  = ellmer::type_string("Name of the testing data frame object in R memory (e.g. 'test_df')"),
    target_var    = ellmer::type_string("Name of the target outcome column to predict (e.g. 'is_high_margin')")
  )
)

#chat <- ellmer::chat("ollama/gemma4")
chat$register_tool(tabpfn_tool)

# Chat execution
chat$chat("I have 'train_df' and 'test_df' objects loaded. Fit a tabpfn model to predict 'is_high_margin' and explain the prediction results to me.")
```

# Discussion

In this notebook:

- TabPFN performs statistical prediction.
- ellmer provides natural-language reasoning and tool orchestration.
- Together they form an AI-assisted analytical workflow.
